title: Two levels of understanding: binah and tevuna, and how contemplation on G-dliness reaches the heart and the deed
overview: Chapter 3 applies the method of the first two chapters to *hisbonenus*, contemplation on G-dliness, and so to davening and to the *avoda* of the heart. The first line names two levels of understanding, *binah* and *tevuna*. *Binah* is grasping an idea in all its details, what it is and how it works, and then going deeper by three steps. Its length is the approach to the idea through the known analogies (*meshalim*). Its width is the difference between those analogies, each one explaining a different aspect of the same idea. Its depth comes only after length and width, because the idea never appears in its essential form, only in external forms. The example throughout is *memalei kol almin*, G-d filling all worlds. From the depth comes *daas*, when the idea is found in oneself, and then *chachma*, seeing it beyond the particulars and beyond creation. *Tevuna* brings the depth back down: seeing G-d's speech in every creature, and so turning understanding into love, fear and action. The chapter ends with the Mitteler Rebbe's complaint that some chassidim learn *Chassidus* and cannot apply it to davening, because their understanding stays a theory.

terms.gloss: contemplation on G-dliness, the process the chapter lays out, from understanding through depth to action
understanding: grasping an idea in all its details, what it is and how it works, and going deeper into it
drawing the idea out: bringing the depth of an idea back down into the physical world and into action
(the light) that fills all worlds; G-d's presence within creation, seen through creation
depth: the distilled essence of an idea, reached only after its length and width
close analysis of the external details, the tool that brings you to the depth
spreading forth from the essence, like the power an agent invests in what it makes
revelation of what is hidden: the essence revealed through an expression, like a sun seen rather than its light
knowledge: the bond with the idea, when it is found in oneself and felt personally
wisdom: the intuition of an idea's general principle, seen beyond the particulars
(the light) that encompasses all worlds; G-d's transcendence over creation, known only by emuna

sections.title: Two levels of understanding in contemplation: binah and tevuna
sections.summary: The chapter applies the theory of the first two chapters to contemplating G-dliness. Its first line names two levels, *binah* and *tevuna*.

phrases.he: (ג) ובכל זה יובן בענין ההתבוננות בהשגת האלקות,
phrases.en: so now we can understand the process of how to properly do *hisbonenus* in a G-dly, in trying to understand G-dliness

phrases.he: שיש ב' מדריגות, בינה ותבונה.
phrases.en: there's two levels of understanding or *hisbonenus*, which correspond to *binah* and *tevuna*

blocks.text: Chapter 3 applies the theory of the first two chapters to contemplating G-dliness, and so to davening and to *avoda*. The principle holds for learning anything. It doesn't have to be this: it could be studying for a calculus exam, and it could also be prayer. What is said here is about how to contemplate a G-dly idea properly.
The line says there are two levels of contemplation. The first is *binah*, and the chapter takes it up first, with its example.

sections.title: Binah, first step: understand the idea in all its details
sections.summary: Whatever you study, you must understand what it is and how it works, with all its parts, spending time on it until you grasp it in depth.

phrases.he: בינה היינו בחינת עצם ההשגה האלקית בכל פרט ענין שמתבונן,
phrases.en: whatever you're studying, whatever G-dly topic you're studying, you have to understand it, and understand it well with all of its details

phrases.he: איך הוא
phrases.en: exactly what it is

phrases.he: ומה הוא,
phrases.en: and how it works

phrases.he: ועומד על הדבר בעיון רב
phrases.en: and spend a lot of time, you know, meditating on it, like dwelling on the idea

phrases.he: בכל פרטי חלקיו
phrases.en: with all of its details, really analyzing it, pulling it apart, understanding it in depth

phrases.he: כו' כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: *Binah* is grasping the G-dly idea itself. Whatever you contemplate, you must understand what it is and how it works, with all its details, dwelling on it and analyzing it until you understand it in depth. That is the first thing. The second comes later, and first he gives an example of what this means for G-dly understanding.

sections.title: Binah, the example: G-d filling all worlds
sections.summary: The example is *memalei kol almin*. Its simplest form is learned by rote; its depth requires seeing how the idea comes from nothing.

blocks.text: Take *memalei kol almin*. The simplest version, learned by rote (*girsa*), is that G-d fills all worlds, is everywhere, just as the soul fills the body, as the *midrash* says. That is where most people stop, and they move on.

The line's concept of creation is *yesh me-ayin*, something from nothing, which is the power of an agent invested in what it makes. The simplest case is throwing a stone. An artist puts something of himself into his work and leaves an imprint you can see.

phrases.he: כמו בהשגה פרטיות דממלא כל עלמין
שהוא התהוות יש מאין
phrases.en: and this is in general the concept of creation, something from nothing

phrases.he: הנקרא כח הפועל האלקי בנפעל כו'
phrases.en: which is also called the *koach hapoel b'nifal*, like the force that's vested in the action

phrases.he: והוא בחינת שם אדנ״י או שם אלהי״ם, לשון כח
phrases.en: the divine name of G-d as a master or the judge of the world, which both imply power and force

phrases.he: כידוע.
הנה יש בזה כמה חלוקי פרטים באופני חיצוניות הענין עד אשר יושג תוך תוך הענין הזה בפנימית העצמי, איך שהוא בעצם כו' שזהו הנקרא עומק המושג
phrases.en: there are a lot of details, all the external forms of the idea, until you reach its inner essence, what it really is; that is called the depth of the concept

phrases.he: כו'

blocks.text: The Name of G-d as Master, and the divine name of *Elokim*, both imply power and force. Looking at creation, the greatness of G-d's handiwork lets us appreciate something of G-d.

Within this idea there are many details, the external forms in which it can be understood. You need to understand them until you reach the inner essence of the idea, what G-d's being fills the worlds really is. That point is the depth of the concept, and it takes many details to get there.

To arrive at the real depth of what it means that G-d fills all worlds, you must study many variations on that theme and understand how they differ and relate. That process gives the length and width, and the length and width let you get to the depth.

blocks.question: Is that comparing and contrasting the variations to abstract the point they share, and the unique facet that sets each apart?
blocks.text: He agrees: something like that.

sections.title: Length: the analogies that bring the idea near the mind
sections.summary: The length is approaching the idea through known analogies, rooted in physical experience a child could grasp, and then climbing to the depth and back down.

blocks.text: Analysis, *iyun*, is the tool that brings you to the depth, since the depth cannot be reached directly. The idea never appears in its essential form, only in external forms, so you must study those external forms until you feel the depth they share. That answers the unspoken question of why one needs *iyun* at all.

phrases.he: כנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: like we explained before

phrases.he: שהעיון הוא בחינת כלי לבא לבחינת העומק כו'
phrases.en: that *iyun*, this analysis, this process of learning the external details and comparing them, contrasting them, doing that whole process, that is the tool that will allow you to reach the depth

blocks.text: The length is the approach to the idea through known *meshalim*. You begin there: you cannot meditate on the *nimshal* (what the analogy stands for) directly. Some people simply picture G-d as one and imagine Him, and without the texts that is what one can do.

The *midrash* on the world as G-d's body: the grass and trees are like hair, the rivers like blood flowing, the whole world a great body with a living spirit. Picture it, walk outside and feel closeness to this greater being. How accurate that picture is can be debated, but at least it is something.
Take a walk outside, in the woods, and spend time thinking about all this. Length means using all these analogies to make the idea close.

The analogy must be close to the mind, something you really see and can point to in your own life. It cannot be something you take on *kabbalas ol*: the key is to make sure you really understand the analogy.

blocks.question: How do you know you have the analogy right? If you say it applies to my life in this way?
blocks.text: He says we are not yet talking about application. For now we are only seeing the analogy clearly; application is the second step.

There are two steps. The first is the process of going up, to the depth. The second, *tevuna*, the application, is coming back down. Before you climb the ladder, make sure it stands on the ground, rooted in real, tangible experiences you can see in your own life.

blocks.title: Raw food and cooked
blocks.text: The *Frierdiker Rebbe* explains the difference between the *avoda* of a *tzaddik* and of a *baal teshuva*, and between *avoda* from above to below and from below to above. The *nefesh hasichis* cannot grasp that difference, so he gives an analogy: vegetables and fruit that you can eat raw, against meat and fish that you need to cook.
The analogy of foods needs no special philosophical or spiritual appreciation. It is a real, physical *mashal* and a fact of daily life, something a person has direct experience of.

Torah is rich in one place and poor in another. Some places explain an analogy at length, others only mention it, so you must learn what each analogy is meant to be. In *Tanya* there are two places with the sun's light as the analogy, and they are not the same analogy.

The Rebbe's index for *Tanya* follows the passage that explains a topic, not every place where the word appears. It lists the two places under one entry, but for the other entry it lists only one. Asked whether that was a mistake, he explained that the two analogies are slightly different, so both apply in one place and not in the other. Finding the difference may take work and research, but once you understand the analogy, anyone without being specially religious or philosophic should be able to see it in the world around them.

The analogy must be in physical form, something a child could understand. A *maamar* or *sicha* that brings an analogy has to give it as a clear physical form that you can point to and explain to a kindergartener, not something you take on *kabbalas ol*. A person of *tevuna* can create such analogies. Here the Rebbe has already given one, and your job is the *iyun* that brings you to its depth.

A joke about two chassidim learning *Torah Or* and *Likkutei Torah*. The text says most of the world is covered with water. One says he has been to Warsaw and Leipzig and seen no such water. The other says that is one of the things you take on *kabbalas ol*.
Sometimes you need to do research to understand what the analogy means physically. Then you can understand the analogy.

blocks.title: Refining silver
blocks.text: A man told him about someone giving a *shiur* who taught the image of refining silver. A listener did not understand it, so he was sent to a jeweler's shop. At the end of the day the jeweler swept the dust from his counters and boiled it in a crucible until it was pure. Asked how he knew it was pure, he said: when he could see his reflection in it.

He saw in the name of the *Ba'al Shem Tov* that G-d made us do business, so that we would deal with people and exchange ideas about Him. Each job gives its own set of analogies for understanding G-d's unity.
When *Chassidus* brings an analogy like the silver, and you know nothing about its background, you may not understand it. So do a little research to understand what the analogy is.

The length is the quality of the first connection to the idea: an experience firmly rooted in your life, physical and tangible, that you can sense and relate to. It should not be a difficult abstract thing. Then comes the second step, the width.

phrases.he: ובחינת האורך
phrases.en: the length of this process

phrases.he: הוא בחינת התקרבות הענין הזה אל השכל במשלים שונים הידועים
עד שיהיה הדבר הזה קרוב במוחו מאד
(בל"א אראפ גילאזן זייער דעם שכל צו זיך)
phrases.en: to really bring the idea, the concept close to you

phrases.he: בלבוש הגשמה,
phrases.en: it has to come in a physical form

phrases.he: עד שיוכל תינוק להשיג כו' כנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: it has to be something that a child could understand

sections.title: Width: many analogies, and how their differences give depth
sections.summary: One idea is explained by several analogies, and each one shows a slightly different aspect. Learning the differences is the width.

blocks.text: The width is to expand the idea as it is, in several ways and not just one. Take the many analogies found in *Chassidus* and *Kabbalah*. Often there are five analogies for one idea. At first glance they seem to say the same thing again and again, poetically, with a different angle and no real change. Look carefully and each analogy explains the idea at a slightly different level.
Each analogy is for a different concept, a different aspect of the same idea. Understanding those differences is what brings you to the depth of the idea.

The same holds when different Rebbeim explain one idea. The Mitteler Rebbe and the Tzemach Tzedek explain it differently, and the distinctions between them give a deeper view of the idea. In one chapter, which he thinks is chapter 12, the Mitteler Rebbe gives five analogies for *tzimtzum* and five for *reshimu*.

How are you supposed to know what the differences are? For most people, especially at the start, the practical way is to find places in *Chassidus* that explain the differences. A *maamar* of the Rebbe Rashab explains the difference between those five analogies.

Here the Mitteler Rebbe says the idea of *memalei kol almin* has nine analogies in two topics, but he does not explain their differences here. A *maamar* called *Zecher Rav Tuvcha* explains them, and the Biur of Reb Hillel Paritcher quotes that *maamar* at length. Without it you would not appreciate the nuance.

There are many places where *Chassidus* makes such distinctions, giving two or three analogies for one idea and explaining that they differ. Amarei Binah, he thinks, goes through this kind of thing a lot. Putting that together is the advantage of breadth of knowledge.

blocks.question: Is that the advantage of breadth of knowledge? You are making me think of girsa and iyun: the main thing seemed to be iyun and the details, but breadth lets you cover the concepts that light up any set of details you are analyzing.
blocks.text: Yes. Breadth of knowledge definitely helps, and so do research skills.

Research skills matter as the Rebbe encouraged. A work with good footnotes can be looked up, sources cross-checked, and the difference between sources analyzed. It is much more work than just reading, but it gives much deeper understanding, and he does not do it as often as he should.
A book that quotes many sources carries hidden shades of meaning in its references and word choice. If you do not know the reference you miss the nuance. It is not just being poetic.

The same holds in *Nigleh*, where people analyze the exact wording of a commentator on the *Shulchan Aruch* and find the nuance in every word. Those authors knew what they were talking about and put a lot into every word.

Someone said he appreciated the Rebbe's *sichos*, but found the footnotes even more interesting. Few people look at the footnotes of a *maamar* or *sicha*, but when you take the time, it is a very different level of study.

The Haggadah of Pesach is scholarly work, mostly footnotes and sources. The Rebbe brought academic research into *Chassidus* and into learning generally, looking at manuscripts and the earlier versions of *Rashi* and *Rambam*, and asking why a text was changed, and whether a change was a mistake. That is the width.

phrases.he: והרוחב היינו להרחיב זה הדבר
phrases.en: the second thing is to expand on the idea

phrases.he: כמו שהוא בכמה אופנים שונים, ולא באופן א' לבד

blocks.text: For the width of *memalei kol almin*, take the analogy of the soul's life in the body, which the *midrash* uses: G-d fills the world as the soul fills the body. But that is only one aspect. When you dig deep, it is a metaphor only for the idea of the essence and of *hispashtus min ha'etzem*, spreading forth from the essence.

phrases.he: כמו המשל לזה הדבר מחיי הנפש בגוף,
phrases.en: the life of the soul in the body

phrases.he: שאין זה רק התפשטות מן העצם כידוע
phrases.en: it's only a metaphor for the idea of *etzem v'hispashtus*, or *hispashtus min ha'etzem*

blocks.text: There are many details in *hispashtus min ha'etzem* within this one aspect. And there is also the other aspect of *memalei kol almin*, which is *gilui ha'helem*, revealing what is hidden, and it has its own analogies.

phrases.he: ויש רבוי אופנים למאוד בהתפשטות מן העצם
phrases.en: just within this one aspect of *memalei kol almin*, there's a lot of details

phrases.he: וגם בגלוי ההעלם,
phrases.en: there's also the other aspect of *memalei kol almin*, which is *gilui ha'helem*, revealing something that's hidden, which has its own metaphors

blocks.text: The analogies for *gilui ha'helem* are movement that shows a living thing, the letters of speech that reveal a thought, wisdom coming from a person's essential wisdom, the sight of the eye, and a flame revealed from an ember. All of these are *gilui ha'helem*.

Against these are the sun's ray, a candle's light and the power of an agent: a person investing some of their power in something, like throwing a stone or doing a craft. These are *hispashtus min ha'etzem*.

blocks.question: Without the analogies, what is the basic difference between the two core concepts?
blocks.text: A student gives the answer. Hispashtus is investing your own power in something. Gilui ha'helem is an expression of a more essential faculty, not the faculty itself but its expression. He agrees there are a couple of basic differences, and the most essential one is the next point.

blocks.title: The dollar from the great-aunt
blocks.text: A little child is given a dollar by a great-aunt he sees once a year. He appreciates the tangible thing and its value, and not the person, whom he does not really know. A more mature person, given a dollar by a Rebbe, values the dollar because it comes from the Rebbe, and values the Rebbe as a *tzaddik*. The less mature person appreciates the physical gift, which can be a gateway to a relationship with the source. The more mature one appreciates the source, and sees that the gift expresses a sentimental value beyond itself.

blocks.title: The sun behind a curtain
blocks.text: Sunlight comes through a very thin curtain. You get its warmth and light and know it comes from a source, but you value the product. Take the curtain away and you see the sun itself: the light now carries an image of the sun to your eye, and the light is only the carrier. That is *gilui ha'helem*: you see the *mahus* of the source.

So with *memalei kol almin* there are two general levels of appreciation. The first is the physical world, how great it is, and how great G-d must be as its creator. That is the external level of *hispashtus min ha'etzem*, which has four levels: *Asiya*, *Yetzira*, *Beriya* and *Atzilus*, and that is why there are four analogies for it.

The deeper level is appreciating the *mahus* of G-dliness. Then the main thing you value in the world is that it is G-d speaking to us, His autobiography, and the physical things are a medium that expresses that higher G-dly revelation. That deeper view is where *hasagas hamahus* is possible.
Bringing that perception down until you see it physically in the world, with the animal soul, is what the revelation of *Moshiach* is about. *Nevuah* relates to it too.

There are four analogies for *hispashtus min ha'etzem* but five for *gilui ha'helem*, because on the level of *hispashtus* you appreciate only the four worlds. In *gilui ha'helem* you also appreciate the fifth, the essence, higher than the four, like *Or Ein Sof*. Compare the *pshat, remez, drush, sod* of *Modeh Ani* with the depth *Chassidus* adds to them: that added depth shifts the reading to *gilui ha'helem*.

He is not explaining it all here. If you go and research it, a simple topic like *memalei kol almin* becomes a whole big topic, and understanding the nuances of its levels takes it to a different level.

blocks.title: Studying the author, not the story
blocks.text: Some people study an author's stories not for their content but to learn the author's style and how his mind works. A biographer might study a composer's works to understand what he felt at a point in his life, as a gateway to appreciating the source, and not just to say that he likes the work.

That is a different level of maturity in our relationship with G-d. Do we value G-d and G-dliness for their essential, intrinsic value, or is it a self-centered, transactional relationship: G-d gives me things I like, so I have to say thank you? That is a deep point.
An American broadcaster, asked how a Jew who believes in G-d will be saved, answered, something like: I believe in serving G-d, not in a G-d who serves me.

There are many shifts in perspective, and seeing how they move between this way and that is what it is about. Each perspective has its advantage and its disadvantage, and with all these nuances *memalei kol almin* becomes a complete ladder of levels. When a person separates from another in their general connection to spirituality and G-dliness, it is these shifts in perspective that make the difference.

sections.title: Depth, daas and chachma: the idea found in oneself, then seen beyond creation
sections.summary: The depth comes only after the length and the width have been worked through, and it is a distillation of the many analogies.

blocks.text: The class opens by recapping: the length, width and depth of *binah* in the example of *memalei kol almin*, and the difference between *kli* and *helem*, and between *etzem v'hispashtus* and *hispashtus min ha'etzem*, each with its own analogies.

All nine analogies explain the essential concept, which is what kind of relationship we are looking for. It is not about applying the understanding to examples in life. It is so that you get clear what we are looking for, and the idea has been expanded.

The opposite of expansion is *kitzur*, shortening. You could simply say that G-d fills the world as the soul fills the body, and move on. You would not have the broad picture or the nuance, and not even that one analogy would be fully understood without comparing it to the others. You cannot tell which parts of the analogy are essential and which are circumstantial.
Without any expansion you get only a definition, which you can repeat but which has no context for interpreting what is meant by it.

phrases.he: הרי כל זה בעצם הענין
phrases.en: so all of these *meshalim*, all these nine *meshalim*, are all explaining the essential concept

phrases.he: רק שנתרחב,
phrases.en: it's just that it became expanded

phrases.he: וההיפך מזה הוא הקיצור
phrases.en: and the opposite of that would be a *kitzur*

phrases.he: רק באופן אחד,
phrases.en: you just get one one understanding of it through one avenue

phrases.he: וגם הוא בדרך קצרה
phrases.en: and even that one explanation is going to be in a very short way

phrases.he: נסקר במוחו בלתי התפשטות להרחיב בו כלל כו'

blocks.text: When a person grasps the depth of the idea itself, after all the many analogies are explained, that is *omek* and the distilled essence of the concept. The length is the quality of each analogy. The width is understanding how they differ, all nine of them. After that whole process, the person can grasp the depth and have a true understanding of what is meant by *memalei kol almin*.

phrases.he: אבל כמו שזה הדבר נתפס לעומקו בעצם,
phrases.en: but when a person gets the real depth, they really grasp the depth of the concept

phrases.he: אחר כל רבוי הסבר דמיון המשלים,
phrases.en: after explaining all of these many *meshalim*

phrases.he: הוא הנקרא עומק ותמצית זה המושג כנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: and that is the depth and the real distilled essence of this concept like we discussed in the previous two chapters

blocks.text: The depth that can be understood from the analogies comes out only through their length and width, and through really analyzing them well. The key point is that understanding G-dliness, and really appreciating it, comes only through this methodical process of learning.

A person who takes one idea and tries to delve into it without enough breadth, seeing how it compares to other things, will make mistakes. He fools himself about the true depth of his understanding, or he just pictures it in his mind.

The Rebbe Rashab wrote to the students of *Tomchei Tmimim* about how to learn *Gemara*. He recommends a course of study, including *Derchei HaGemara*. He says not to aim at making *chiddushim*, new explanations, but to understand the text well, first according to *Rashi* and then *Tosafos*, and the difference between them. Then, if you get a new insight, it will be true, because it comes from the deep understanding.
If a person invents ideas and forces explanations beyond what he has mastered, it will in all likelihood be off center.

The depth is abstract. So a person can only get that depth after first grasping the idea as it is expressed externally, in these physical forms and analogies, and analyzing them all. Without focusing first on the analogies and understanding the differences between them, one cannot reach the depth. That is the length, width and depth of *binah* in this *hisbonenus*.

phrases.he: ודווקא אחר האריכות והרוחב במשלים בעיון רב יבא לבחינת העומק
phrases.en: it's only through the length and the width of all these *meshalim* and really analyzing the *meshalim* very well, can a person get the depth

phrases.he: שמובן מהם,
phrases.en: that can be understood from them

blocks.text: *Daas* is the recognition and feeling of the understood idea, bonded to it. It is when the idea is not just something you read in a textbook but something you can see, sense and feel personally.

phrases.he: ובחי' הדעת הוא בחינת ההכרה והרגשה במושכל

blocks.text: The verse says: know today, and know the G-d of your father. The only way to have *daas* in G-dliness is through studying *memalei kol almin* specifically, because there you see how G-dliness is revealed through creation. That you can see and know directly and experience, not just theory or philosophy.

blocks.question: Is it because we understand something concretely that we take an interest in it, since we tend to be interested in what we relate to through direct experience?
blocks.text: Yes. You see that it is personally relevant, and that understanding G-dliness helps you be your real self and connect to it in a personal way.

You understand it through the analogies, and then you find it in yourself. Once you connect to G-dliness and find the G-dly spark in yourself, which is the *yechida*, you gain the intuition for the next stage, *chachma*, which is beyond *daas*.

Books advertise mastering their knowledge for your health, your relationships, your money. The insight is that you can tap into something greater than all of those, which is the more essential reality, the G-dly soul. All of those things are a vehicle for expressing it.

phrases.he: ועל זה נאמר
phrases.en: and this is what it says

phrases.he: וידעת כו'
phrases.en: you should know today

phrases.he: דע את אלה״י כו'
phrases.en: you have to know the G-d of your father

phrases.he: שהוא בהשגה זו דממלא כל עלמין דוקא כידוע
phrases.en: the only way that a person could have *daas* in G-dliness is through studying *memalei kol almin* specifically

blocks.text: *Hayom Yom* gives three steps in *hisbonenus*: understand the idea well, intellectually; sense the *chayus*, the life in the idea; and appreciate the G-dliness in it. *Binah* is the first, *daas* is sensing the life in it, and *chachma* is appreciating the intrinsic value of G-dliness beyond how it is for you personally.

The depth of *chachma* is what brings a person to the depth of everything, from *ayin*. This is the difference between *memalei kol almin* and *sovev kol almin*. Seeing G-d in creation is *memalei kol almin*. Seeing how G-d transcends creation is *sovev kol almin*, which cannot be had through *daas* but only through *emuna*.

*Emuna* is relating to G-d as beyond time and space and every limitation of creation. You cannot directly see that, but by first understanding G-dliness within creation you come to recognize that it is more abstract than creation. Once you have the depth of *binah*, you start to see a general principle deeper than the examples. That is how you go from *binah* to *chachma*.

blocks.question: Is it inference, like a scientist who learns the mechanics of the brain and sees how much more there is that he does not know?
blocks.text: It depends on the kind of inference. The point is that you begin to get the fundamental principles that generalize to many things. That is *chachma*, and it happens in science and mathematics, and in anything, when you get an insight beyond the particulars you learned.

phrases.he: (בל"א דער קלעפ כו' כנ"ל באורך)
שהוא דוקא המביא לבחינת עומקא דכולא,
phrases.en: and this is what brings a person to the depth of everything

phrases.he: דהיינו לעומק דחכמה
phrases.en: or the depth of *chachma*

phrases.he: שמאין תמצא כנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: which comes from the *ayin*, like we said before, it's this higher, more abstract idea

blocks.text: Within the depth of *chachma*, the mind's eye sees the truth of an idea as if it were a direct experience, beyond what the intellect itself grasps. It is the depth of seeing from the mind's eye in this grasp of *memalei kol almin*, which lies above the grasp of the intellect.

There is what you can explain, and there is the truth you see beyond explanation, completely obvious to you even though you cannot explain it. That comes from seeing the idea in yourself first, which is *daas*.

A child in school learns the algebra formula to distribute binomials, memorizes it without knowing why, and passes the test without seeing the truth. Once you study an idea deeply you gain its intuition, and you feel that you just know it, the way you see something with your eyes.

blocks.question: So you mean someone who memorizes a formula and applies it to solve a problem, as opposed to understanding what the formula represents more broadly?
blocks.text: Yes. Once you reach a certain point, one plus one not equaling two would scream against your intuition. It is not a truth you understand only in specific problems. You see its intuition.

A lot of times people have a strong sense of intuition about an idea even though they cannot explain or prove it. A famous debate: does 0.999 repeated forever equal one? Intuition says no, since something is not added and it should go on forever. Many proofs show it does equal one, and most mathematicians say so. Yet people argue strongly that it does not, because there is more than one perspective on that question, and depending on which one you come from, it is obvious to you one way or the other.

Until a person has enough understanding to see the assumptions, each side just knows it is right. You cannot dissuade people with an argument, because they see the truth as if with their eyes, even though it is an intellectual thing. That is dangerous when something cannot be subjected to rigorous analysis: someone can take some sort of substance, G-d forbid, and believe he perceives something intuitively, and then be closed-minded and keep believing in mumbo-jumbo.

It is not that such intuition cannot be explained, only that the person is not able to right now. That is why in *halacha* a person must be able to explain his reasoning before he is relied on as a decisor. Rabbi Meir had a deeper perspective than many other *tannaim*, but his rulings are not always followed, because they could not follow his perspective.

The sense of the truth comes before the explanation. Once a person has that depth of experience, they know what is right because of it, and when asked why, they have to think how to bring it down and explain it. They know it from a deeper perspective than conscious thought.

At Sinai the Jewish people all had this level of seeing, but it was possible only because at the splitting of the Red Sea they first had *daas* of G-dliness, seeing it in the physical world through the miracle. Without that physical experience first, they could not reach the level of Sinai.

So the first stage is the process of going up. First study the analogies and the differences between them, and so reach the depth of the idea. Then stop and ask how it relates to you: what would my life look like if I viewed the world from this perspective, and how is it a powerful, important thing in my life? When you find that in yourself, you become aware of your G-dly soul, and the shell of *kelipas nogah* over it begins to crack. Then you can have a direct perception, at the level of *chachma*, and G-d becomes something you see in the world around you.

blocks.question: So the starting point is asking what your life would be like if you understood this stuff, before you have understood it?
blocks.text: The teacher says that a person who does not yet know enough cannot know what he is missing. A student suggests looking at great *tzaddikim* who knew the subject and had an impact on the world, and being moved by them to want to know it.

At the start a person is led by a teacher and does it with *kabbalas ol*, the way a child is made to learn to read before he can see the benefit of reading. Then: study the subject in *binah* first. After that, stop and find it in yourself and in your life, and how it could change you. That gives the deeper perspective of *chachma*, from the G-dly soul. Then *tevuna* comes, and it takes practice: you can pick something in the world and break it down on the nine levels of *memalei kol almin*.

blocks.title: Only G-d exists
blocks.text: A chassid who became a Rebbe himself, returning from time spent learning from the *Maggid* of Mezeritch (he is not sure whether it was the Alter Rebbe or the Berditchever Rebbe), was asked by his father-in-law what he had learned. He said that after all that time he had learned that only G-d exists. The father-in-law said even the simplest person knows that, and asked a woman in the house, who said yes. The chassid said: she says that only G-d exists, but I now actually know it. That difference is a totally different quality of life.

*Chovos HaLevavos* begins with its *Shaar HaYichud*, on levels of appreciating G-d's unity. The first, most basic, level is saying *Shema Yisrael* without knowing what the words mean, and then the obligation is to develop an understanding of it.

A student recalls that in *Tanya* the Alter Rebbe discusses the practical *mitzvos*, perhaps the etrog, and says that only through their action do you relate to G-d's essence. He also seems to say that the detailed knowledge of how G-d brings all into being from nothing, the *hishtalshelus*, is a *mitzvah* exalted above all. He is not sure how the two fit. He suggests that the objective reality is one thing and the subjective human experience of it is what this study aligns, so the knowledge is exalted for that reason.

*Tanya* says there is an advantage to the practical *mitzvos*, but also to this understanding: it brings a person to a *lev shalem*, a complete heart, so that love, fear and the motivation are sincere, and a person does the *mitzvos* because he wants to, not only because he must. That spiritual maturity comes through understanding G-d's unity and the *mitzvos*.

blocks.title: A book about a compulsion
blocks.text: He mentions a book, *The Devil is in the Details*, and a woman who went through Asperger's and still had the compulsion. She started reading the Bible, and it impelled her to certain actions. She misunderstood a lot of what she read, but something in her saw these things, a compulsion of the eye of her *sechel*, the way the soul responds before the mind understands.

Once a person has the complete understanding, he can be a vessel for it, so the mind's eye can see it consciously, and it stays with him rather than coming and going.

blocks.title: The hat
blocks.text: A friend always wore a hat. In the 1950s and 1960s, wearing a hat at school or in a courthouse went against the grain, and people had trouble with a *yarmulke*, a beard, in the army. Yet people without any understanding, even without knowing they were Jewish, latched onto certain things, *kashrus* or *Shabbos*.

blocks.text: The woman who went through a great deal of strangeness was introduced to a Modern Orthodox Jew. Sitting with her, the structure she had been imposing on herself made sense, and she was able to normalize her life, without all the swings and craziness.

sections.title: Tevuna: drawing the depth back down into the world
sections.summary: Tevuna is bringing the depth of the idea back into physical life: seeing in each creature the letters of G-d's speech, so that the understanding does not stay a theory.

blocks.text: The next class opens by recapping the three stages of *binah*, *daas* and *chachma*, and now turns to *tevuna*.

*Tevuna* is drawing out the depth of the idea from its hidden place into revelation. Once the idea has been understood in *binah* and found in oneself, the person can get a higher perception of it, like *yichuda ila'a*, which is *chachma*.

Then the person can apply what he understands: he sees it in everything around him, and that leads to *ahava* and *yirah* and to actions influenced by it. Because he has absorbed the meaning of the idea and internalized it, he can start seeing it in everything, in each detail of the world.

So *tevuna* lets you see, in each detail of the creatures, how each one comes from nothing into being. Hidden in the general understanding of *memalei kol almin* is the ability to see every detail of how each creature, and everything we experience, is created by G-d.
Without this *tevuna*, the grasp of the idea stays only in the mind's understanding. It stays a theory, something that talks about books but is not something you see in the world around you.
A person who lacks that *tevuna* does not know how to apply it, or how to bring this *hisbonenus* into the world around him, to see how things come into being from nothing.

blocks.text: This explains why some new chassidim, and even some older ones, cannot apply their *hisbonenus*. The Mitteler Rebbe says they come and complain to him: what is all this *Chassidus* good for, and how do you use it in davening? They learn the *maamarim* and understand them, but only as something separate from the world. Even understanding very fine ideas, they cannot bring them into contemplation in *tefilla* on how the worlds are created.

The questioner asks what to do with all this and what it is for. To him there are two separate worlds: the theory of *Chassidus*, which seems just an intellectual thing, and the world of davening and feelings. The understanding remains only as a theory, detached from anything in the world, just the idea by itself.

That is enough to understand the basic idea: through *hisbonenus* we unlock all of these things. When it is done properly it unlocks the love and fear, and the actions in davening and *avoda*. It is not separate from them at all.

notes.text: The Biur. The class goes into Reb Hillel Paritcher's Biur at 012 words 1097-1105 ('let's take a look at this biur'), and its text starts at word 1106 ('u-me'ata yesh lehavin', pp. 316-317 in the class's page count). The classes call it Likutei Biurim and say it is 'in the back of the book'. The stretch is omitted under 'other', as the series owner decided. The Biur does explain the chapter's examples in places (the teacher says so at 812-829 and 975-995); a reviewer may decide that a stretch truly explains a chapter line, and cite it then. The teacher's own summary at 5438-5547 is cited by a block (keyPoint, placed at the end with outOfPlace).
Line 1: the class reads 'mevuan inyan hisbonenus' where the line says 'uvechol zeh yuvan'. His English ('so now we can understand') follows the reading, and the line stays the text.
Line 21 is not read in any of the three classes. In class 011 (words 2138-2151) he says 'like it says in Raaya Mehemna... oh no, I skipped', and it is left without a passage's blocks.
He thinks the five analogies for tzimtzum and reshimu are in chapter 12 ('I think it might be chapter 12 or so'). Not confirmed; written as he hedged.

Lines 11-12 are rendered piece by piece over 010 words 4341-4502. Line 3's 'let's say you're going to study the topic of memalei kol almin' is not a rendering and is left Hebrew-only.

The 3507 question is a student's (the teacher answers it at 3579 and later); the student's suggestion of examples of tzaddikim (3606-3701) is attributed to the student in the block.
